walkthroughs.body_html:
States of Matter — a core area of GCSE Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

States of Matter brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with States of Matter.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
A hydrogen bond is a bond formed when hydrogen molecules fuse together.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.

mcqs.q: How do alkenes typically react with bromine?
options: By electrophilic addition — bromine adds across the double bond to form a dibromoalkane.
Bromine substitutes for a hydrogen on the alkene, releasing HBr.
A hydrogen bond is a bond formed when hydrogen molecules fuse together.
The alkene polymerises with bromine to form a long chain.
A hydrogen bond is a covalent bond involving hydrogen.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
A strong dipole-dipole interaction between an H atom bonded to N/O/F and a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
A hydrogen bond is a bond formed when hydrogen molecules fuse together.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Melting”?
options: Particles far apart, moving fast and randomly in all directions.
Liquid → gas at the boiling point; particles gain enough energy to escape forces between them.
Solid → liquid at the melting point; energy breaks regular structure.
Particles close together but able to flow past each other.
